title.narrative: Advancing human-wildlife conflict management effectiveness in Kenya through an integrated approach

description.narrative: 1. At the 1992 Earth Summit, the Governments of the world agreed on a new agenda for sustainable development which included the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) which, among others, called on governments to establish systems of protected areas and to manage these in support of conservation, sustainable use and equitable socio-economic benefit sharing[1]Governments recognized protected areas as socio-economic institutions that have a key role in alleviating poverty and maintaining the global community’s critical life-support systems. This vision for protected areas requires an awareness and understanding of their socio-economic values and ensuring their protection. 2. The project plays a vital role in improving the management of natural resources in Kenya’s Laikipia, Meru and Taita Taveta (Tsavo) landscapes. By addressing human-wildlife conflicts and supporting sustainable livelihoods, the project enhances economic benefits through increased tourism revenue, alternative livelihoods, and improved agricultural methods. These improvements contribute to the overall resilience of local economies and support the well-being of the population, demonstrating the interconnectedness of natural resource management and economic development with a focus on wildlife economies. The project will improve wildlife management approaches by integrating comprehensive strategies and enhancing capacity. It will strengthen adaptive capacity through flexible management practices and community involvement. It reduces vulnerability by improving buffer capacities and infrastructure. Lastly, it enhances resilience by promoting self-regulation, learning, and innovation, ensuring that the protected area system can effectively anticipate, absorb, and recover from disturbances while maintaining its essential functions and capacity for adaptation. 3. In order to deliver the socio-economic benefits of the project, the following will be taken into account during project implementation: · Climate Resilience: The project integrates climate adaptation strategies into wildlife management and community practices. This includes promoting climate-smart nature-based enterprises and sustainable land use practices that help communities adapt to changing climate conditions and reduce their vulnerability to climate-related shocks. By improving ecosystem health and functionality, the project enhances the ability of natural systems to provide essential services, such as water regulation and soil fertility, which are critical for maintaining resilience in the face of climate variability. The project’s focus on reducing human-wildlife conflicts minimizes the risk of economic losses from wildlife-related damage, which helps communities better manage the impacts of climate change on their livelihoods.· Ecological Resilience: The project includes measures to protect and restore critical wildlife habitats. This enhances ecological resilience by ensuring that ecosystems can withstand and recover from disturbances, such as droughts or floods. By establishing and maintaining wildlife corridors, the project ensures that wildlife can migrate and adapt to changing conditions, which supports the overall resilience of ecological systems. The project’s efforts to conserve diverse species and ecosystems strengthen the resilience of ecological systems by maintaining functional and diverse habitats that are better able to cope with environmental changes.· Social-Ecological Resilience: The project engages local communities in conservation efforts, which builds social resilience by empowering people to manage and protect their natural resources. Community involvement ensures that conservation measures are culturally relevant and supported by those directly affected. By addressing human-wildlife conflicts effectively, the project reduces the social stress and economic impacts associated with wildlife damage. This enhances social resilience by improving community well-being and reducing conflict-related tensions. The project includes training and capacity-building activities for local communities and conservation practitioners, which strengthens their ability to adapt to and manage both ecological and social changes.· Improved Management Frameworks: The project implements integrated management frameworks that combine wildlife conservation with community development, enhancing the effectiveness of resource management. This includes developing and applying best practices for managing human-wildlife interactions and monitoring ecological health. The project employs adaptive management strategies that allow for flexibility and adjustment based on monitoring and evaluation results. This approach ensures that management practices remain effective and responsive to changing conditions. By working with local institutions and stakeholders, the project strengthens governance structures and enhances the capacity for effective resource management, leading to improved outcomes and more sustainable benefits.· Food Security: The project supports the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices that increase productivity and resilience to climate change. This includes promoting techniques that reduce conflicts with wildlife, such as using wildlife-proof fencing and alternative crops. By providing support for alternative livelihoods, the project reduces dependence on agriculture and livestock, thereby decreasing the pressure on natural resources and enhancing food security through diversified income sources. Improved management of natural resources helps to ensure the availability of essential resources, such as water and fertile land, which are crucial for maintaining food security in the face of environmental changes. [1] IUCN 1998. Economic Values of Protected Areas: Guidelines for Protected Area Managers. IUCN, Gland, Switzerland and Cambridge, UK.
